# Crossing the Trough: A Subscription Transition That Keeps the Base, the Sales Force, and the Board

The competitor didn't lose 20% of its installed base because it moved to subscription. It lost 20% because it **forced a decision**. Every forced decision point — "convert or lose your software" — invites the customer to re-evaluate the entire vendor relationship, including alternatives. So the governing design rule for this plan:

> **No customer ever faces a forced decision without a value-preserving path.** Grandfather the asset; retire the economics of staying on it.

The trough itself is not avoidable — it's mechanical (upfront recognition becomes ratable recognition). What you choose is its **shape**: depth versus duration. The evidence from Adobe, Autodesk, and PTC says compress it. A three-year transition with one honest guidance reset beats a five-year drift every time, because investors discount *uncertainty*, not decline.

---

## 1. Offer Structure and Migration Incentives

**Dual-track with a published end date.** Launch subscription alongside perpetual, announce early that new perpetual sales end on a date certain (12+ months' notice), and let relative economics and a widening feature gap do the persuading. The license stays valid forever; what ends is the wisdom of staying on it.

**Segment the installed base and migrate each segment differently:**

| Segment | Offer | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **On maintenance/paid upgrades** | Convert at maintenance-parity pricing, locked 2–3 years; credit any prepaid maintenance | Converts existing recurring revenue ~1:1 — barely deepens the trough and makes switching nearly free |
| **Lapsed maintenance** | Amnesty: no back-fees, year-one discount off subscription list | These seats generate ~$0 today. Recapture is pure upside — often 30–50% of the base |
| **Recent buyers (<12–18 months)** | License purchase price credited across a 3-year subscription | Defuses the angriest cohort before they organize against you |
| **Holdouts / regulated buyers** | Perpetual remains available at a rising price until end-of-sale; maintenance-only after; offer "subscription with perpetual fallback" — 3 consecutive years earns a perpetual right to the then-current version on exit | Directly answers the "rental forever" objection that killed the competitor |

**Pull, don't push.** Ship cloud-connected capabilities (collaboration, AI features, integrations) subscription-only. The narrative must be *"we're investing where the value is compounding,"* not *"we want your money forever."* Pause license audits during the transition — nothing poisons a migration offer like an audit letter in the same quarter.

---

## 2. Pricing: Balancing Trough Depth Against Adoption

Anchor on an illustrative unit: **$10,000 license + 20% maintenance ($2,000/yr)**.

- **Subscription list ≈ 40–50% of license price** ($4,000–5,000/yr). Customers pay less upfront, more over five years; you get predictable, expandable revenue.
- **Steer with relative price, not deep discounts.** Raise perpetual list and maintenance (20% → 22–25%) during the dual-track window rather than discounting subscription into the floor. List-price discounting trains addicts; relative repricing steers.
- **Concentrate generosity in migration credits** — one-time, time-boxed, with sunset clauses and deal-desk approval. This buys adoption speed without resetting long-term ARPU.
- **Discount term, not price.** Push 3-year commitments with annual upfront billing. This protects cash (GAAP revenue falls further than cash under ratable recognition), builds RPO/backlog, and gives investors the visibility they're paying a multiple for.
- **Compression over shallowness.** The trough's depth is fixed by mechanics; its duration is your choice. Target: >50% of new bookings subscription by end of Year 1, >85% by end of Year 2, revenue floor around 75–85% of peak in Year 2 (maintenance conversion cushions it), prior revenue peak recovered in Year 4 — with double the recurring mix and a larger terminal ARR from recapture, expansion, and reduced non-compliance.

---

## 3. Sales Compensation Redesign

Reps don't sabotage subscriptions out of malice; they follow the comp plan. A $10K perpetual deal credits $10K; a $4.5K subscription credits $4.5K — you've asked the sales force to take a 60% pay cut per deal. Fix the math, and behavior follows.

- **Flip comp the same day the offer launches.** Changing it early invites sandbagging; late invites perpetual-selling.
- **Pay on total contract value (TCV).** A 3-year subscription at $4.5K/yr credits $13.5K — *more* than the perpetual deal. The comp plan now sells the transition for you.
- **Accelerator on subscription ACV:** 2x credit in Year 1, stepping down to 1.5x, then 1.25x. Budget this overhang as a disclosed transition cost.
- **Migration quota:** 20–30% of variable comp tied to converting each rep's installed-base book, with time-boxed SPIFFs in the first two quarters to seed referenceable wins.
- **Protect the earners:** 12-month income floor/draw so nobody starves while their book converts; retention bonuses for the top decile — the trough is exactly when competitors recruit your best reps.
- **Clawback on 12-month churn** of migrated accounts, so reps migrate *ready* customers, not just *signed* ones.
- **Split renewals from hunting.** Move renewals to a specialist/CS motion at reduced rates; pay reps new-business rates on expansion.
- **Channel, if you have one:** resellers lose the big upfront invoice. Replace it with a per-seat migration bounty plus trailing residuals, or the channel will keep selling perpetual — or worse, your competitor's product.

One structural point most perpetual companies miss: **you have no renewal muscle.** The first renewal cliff arrives ~12 months after launch, exactly when investors are watching renewal rates. Stand up onboarding, customer success, and usage telemetry in Phase 0 — before the cohort you need to renew exists.

---

## 4. Financial Communication: Keeping Investors and the Board Committed

You can't avoid the trough; you can only decide whether investors can see the bottom. The playbook is **one reset, a new scoreboard, then beat it quarterly.**

**Before announcement (T-2 quarters):**
- Build the metric infrastructure first — ARR, RPO/backlog, net revenue retention, cohort churn. Promising metrics you can't produce is how credibility dies in quarter two.
- Secure liquidity (revolver) sized to the bear-case trough.
- Re-anchor executive comp to transition milestones (ARR, migration rate) instead of EPS. If leadership bonuses depend on short-term earnings, leadership will flinch at the

run.userPrompt:
A software company sells perpetual licenses with paid upgrades, producing lumpy revenue that investors discount heavily. Leadership wants to move to subscriptions, but modeling shows a multi-year revenue trough during the transition, the sales force is paid on large upfront deals, and long-standing customers feel entitled to the licenses they already bought. A competitor that switched abruptly lost a fifth of its installed base.

Plan the business-model transition to subscription revenue. Define the offer structure and migration incentives for existing license holders, the pricing that balances trough depth against adoption, the sales compensation redesign, and the financial communication plan that keeps investors and the board committed through the trough.
